title: Benchmarking Machine Learning Emulators of Stellar Evolution for Precision Asteroseismology
comment: 16 pages, 10 figures, accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal
summary: Fast and accurate stellar evolution emulators---surrogate models that approximate expensive simulation outputs with machine learning (ML)---are powerful tools for modern stellar characterization, hierarchical inference, and population synthesis. We analyze the grid density required for reliable emulation by training ML algorithms on main-sequence models with masses M=[0.7,1.2] solar masses. This range is challenging to emulate due to rapidly varying evolutionary behavior caused by the radiative-to-convective core transition, as well as the requirement to match the part-per-thousand seismic precision that has been delivered for such stars from the NASA Kepler mission. Generating grids from analytical models, as well as MESA, YREC, MIST, and ASTEC, we compare linear interpolation, k-nearest neighbors, random forests, and neural networks (NNs) in interpolating the stellar observables: T_eff, L, Delta nu, and nu_max. While NNs outperform other methods, sparse grids induce localized failures in the core-transition region, resulting in unstable derivatives, ensemble disagreement, and fragmented posterior distributions during inference. Performance gains from denser grids are non-uniform, suggesting that adaptive grid generation should be favored over uniform refinement. Finally, we show that NN ensembles allow for localized uncertainty propagation, more accurately reflecting emulator reliability across parameter space than global uncertainty estimates. As we consider only the two-dimensional case of varying only stellar mass and age along the main sequence, these results represent a lower bound on the challenge in emulating stellar evolution simulations for precision asteroseismology.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes the grid density required for reliable machine-learning-based stellar evolution emulation for main-sequence stars in the mass range 0.7–1.2 M_sun, comparing multiple ML methods and stellar evolution codes. It finds that neural networks outperform other methods but suffer localized failures near the radiative-to-convective core transition on sparse grids, and recommends adaptive grid generation and NN ensembles for localized uncertainty propagation.
AI.motivation: To determine the grid density requirements for accurate stellar evolution emulation, particularly in the challenging mass range where the radiative-to-convective core transition causes rapidly varying evolutionary behavior, and to match the part-per-thousand seismic precision achieved by the Kepler mission.
AI.method: Training multiple ML algorithms (linear interpolation, k-nearest neighbors, random forests, neural networks) on stellar evolution grids generated from analytical models and four codes (MESA, YREC, MIST, ASTEC) to interpolate observables T_eff, L, Δν, and ν_max for main-sequence models with M=[0.7,1.2] M_sun as a function of stellar mass and age.
AI.result: Neural networks outperform other methods. Sparse grids cause localized failures near the core-transition region, leading to unstable derivatives, ensemble disagreement, and fragmented posterior distributions. Performance gains from denser grids are non-uniform, favoring adaptive grid generation over uniform refinement. NN ensembles enable localized uncertainty propagation that more accurately reflects emulator reliability.
AI.conclusion: Since only the two-dimensional case (stellar mass and age along the main sequence) was considered, the results represent a lower bound on the challenge of emulating stellar evolution simulations for precision asteroseismology, and adaptive grid strategies combined with NN ensembles are recommended for robust emulation.

title: The scarcity of white dwarf-brown dwarf binaries in the solar neighbourhood: A population synthesis study
comment: 17 pages, 15 figures, 2 tables; accepted for publication in A&A
summary: White dwarf--brown dwarf (WD--BD) binaries are intrinsically rare systems that provide a unique opportunity to study binary evolution and the formation of substellar companions. Despite recent observational progress, only a small number are known in the solar neighbourhood. We investigate whether their scarcity can be explained by binary formation and evolution together with observational selection effects. We extend the MRBIN binary population synthesis code into the substellar regime by incorporating brown dwarf evolutionary models and an extended initial mass function. We simulate the stellar population within 100 pc of the Sun and compare the predicted WD--BD population with the observed sample. Our simulations predict 13+-5 WD--BD systems within 100 pc, consistent with observations. These systems represent only 0.1% of the local white dwarf population, confirming their rarity. The models reproduce the overall distributions of white dwarf masses, temperatures, and orbital periods, although the simulated brown dwarfs are systematically hotter than observed. Close WD--BD binaries are underproduced with the standard common-envelope efficiency 0.3, suggesting that higher efficiencies may be required to reproduce the observed short-period systems. The simulations also reproduce the observed deficit of systems at intermediate orbital periods between post-common-envelope binaries and wide non-interacting systems, as well as a weakened brown dwarf desert in main-sequence--brown dwarf binaries.

AI.tldr: This paper uses binary population synthesis simulations to investigate why white dwarf-brown dwarf (WD-BD) binaries are so rare in the solar neighbourhood, predicting 13±5 such systems within 100 pc—consistent with observations—and finding they represent only ~0.1% of local white dwarfs.
AI.motivation: WD-BD binaries are intrinsically rare and provide unique insights into binary evolution and substellar companion formation, but only a small number are known in the solar neighbourhood, motivating an investigation into whether their scarcity can be explained by formation/evolution physics and observational selection effects.
AI.method: The authors extend the MRBIN binary population synthesis code into the substellar regime by incorporating brown dwarf evolutionary models and an extended initial mass function. They simulate the stellar population within 100 pc and compare predicted WD-BD systems against the observed sample.
AI.result: Simulations predict 13±5 WD-BD systems within 100 pc, consistent with observations. These represent only 0.1% of the local WD population. Models reproduce observed distributions of WD masses, temperatures, and orbital periods, though simulated BDs are systematically hotter. Close binaries are underproduced with standard common-envelope efficiency of 0.3, implying higher efficiencies may be needed. The simulations also reproduce the observed deficit at intermediate orbital periods and a weakened brown dwarf desert in MS-BD binaries.
AI.conclusion: The scarcity of WD-BD binaries in the solar neighbourhood can largely be explained by binary formation and evolution physics combined with observational selection effects, confirming their intrinsic rarity, though common-envelope efficiency may need revision to reproduce short-period systems.

title: Infrared-excess sources in VVV: candidate debris discs, SED characterization, and variability analysis
comment: 10 pages, 7 figures, 2 tables. Published in MNRAS
summary: Debris disks around main-sequence stars provide important insights into planetary formation and evolution; however, identifying these systems in the Galactic plane, where high interstellar extinction and source crowding are significant, remains challenging. Deep, wide-area surveys such as the VISTA Variables in the Via Lactea (VVV) ESO Public Survey provide multi-epoch infrared observations, enabling systematic searches in these environments. We present a method to construct a refined sample of main-sequence candidates by cross-matching data from Gaia DR3, GLIMPSE, DECaPS, and VIRAC2, to identify infrared excesses through spectral energy distribution (SED) analysis, and to analyse time-series data to detect variability potentially associated with circumstellar material or other astrophysical phenomena. Although infrared excess is commonly associated with debris disks, contributions from unresolved binaries or line-of-sight contamination cannot be excluded. Applying this methodology to the VVV tile d077 using the VIRAC2 catalogue, we analyse an initial sample of 879,556 sources and identify 446 sources flagged by the VO SED Analyser (VOSA) excess-detection algorithm as having infrared excess, of which 171 show candidate periodic variability in the VIRAC2 Ks-band light curves. We further perform SED fitting using theoretical models to derive physical parameters and approximate spectral types for these sources. This work provides a catalogue of infrared-excess candidates in a Galactic field affected by high extinction, along with a reproducible method suitable for future large-scale applications.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a reproducible methodology for identifying main-sequence debris disk candidates in the highly extincted Galactic plane by cross-matching multi-wavelength catalogs (Gaia DR3, GLIMPSE, DECaPS, VIRAC2), detecting infrared excess via SED analysis (VOSA), and finding variability in VIRAC2 Ks-band light curves. Applied to VVV tile d077, it narrows 879,556 sources to 446 infrared-excess candidates, of which 171 show candidate periodic variability, with SED fitting used to derive physical parameters and spectral types.
AI.motivation: Debris disks are crucial for understanding planetary formation and evolution, but identifying them in the Galactic plane is difficult due to high interstellar extinction and source crowding. The authors aim to overcome these challenges using deep, multi-epoch infrared surveys like VVV to systematically search for these systems.
AI.method: The method involves three main steps: (1) cross-matching data from Gaia DR3, GLIMPSE, DECaPS, and VIRAC2 to build a refined sample of main-sequence star candidates; (2) constructing spectral energy distributions (SEDs) and using the VOSA excess-detection algorithm to identify infrared excess; and (3) analysing VIRAC2 Ks-band time-series data to detect periodic variability potentially associated with circumstellar material. SED fitting with theoretical models is then used to derive physical parameters and approximate spectral types.
AI.result: From an initial 879,556 sources in VVV tile d077, 446 were flagged with infrared excess by VOSA, and 171 of these exhibit candidate periodic variability in Ks-band light curves. SED fitting provided physical parameters and approximate spectral types for these sources, yielding a catalogue of infrared-excess candidates in a high-extinction Galactic field.
AI.conclusion: The work delivers a catalogue of infrared-excess candidates in the Galactic plane and a reproducible methodology applicable to future large-scale surveys. It notes that while infrared excess is commonly indicative of debris disks, contributions from unresolved binaries or line-of-sight contamination cannot be excluded, so the candidates require follow-up confirmation.

title: Bifurcations in the Heliosphere: Global-scale Coronal Pseudostreamer Evolution and the Creation of Secondary Heliospheric Current Sheets
comment: 16 pages 8 figures Accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: The heliospheric current sheet (HCS) is the boundary between open magnetic fields of opposite polarity in the solar wind that connect back to their respective open flux regions in the corona. The HCS is often described as a disc-like sheet warped by the combined effects of the inclination of the magnetic equator on the Sun, solar rotation, and solar wind expansion. The HCS is an extension of the helmet streamer belt-the closed-flux region resulting from the global dipole component of the observed photospheric magnetic field. In the absence of a strong dipole, a dominant quadrupole can result in two separate HCSs. Here we report on a set of idealized, axisymmetric solar wind simulations designed to study the transition of the single-HCS corona and inner heliosphere into a multiple-HCS configuration, run with the WindPredict-AW PLUTO MHD code. We systematically vary the relative strengths of the dipole/quadrupole contributions to the global field and show this results in the formation of a large-scale, closed-flux pseudostreamer that interacts with the ambient solar wind. We find that when the dipole and quadrupole magnitudes are approximately equal, our model corona can oscillate between a one- and two-HCS configuration on the timescale of days-to-weeks. We characterize the plasma dynamics of the transition of a global-scale pseudostreamer into a localized, secondary helmet-streamer belt with its own HCS surrounding a newly-opened, opposite-polarity coronal hole. We discuss the implications of our results for solar cycle evolution and the dynamic coupling of the highly structured corona and inner heliosphere.

AI.tldr: The paper uses idealized axisymmetric MHD simulations (WindPredict-AW PLUTO) to study the transition from a single heliospheric current sheet (HCS) to multiple HCSs by varying the relative strengths of dipole and quadrupole contributions to the global solar magnetic field. When the dipole and quadrupole magnitudes are approximately equal, the model corona oscillates between one- and two-HCS configurations on timescales of days to weeks, characterized by the formation and breakup of a large-scale pseudostreamer and a secondary helmet-streamer belt with its own HCS surrounding a newly opened opposite-polarity coronal hole.
AI.motivation: To understand how the corona and inner heliosphere transition from a single-HCS configuration (typical of a strong global dipole) into a multiple-HCS configuration (which can arise when a dominant quadrupole field is present), and to characterize the plasma dynamics and timescales of this topological restructuring, with implications for solar cycle evolution and corona-heliosphere coupling.
AI.method: The authors perform a set of idealized, axisymmetric solar wind simulations using the WindPredict-AW PLUTO MHD code. They systematically vary the relative strengths of the dipole and quadrupole contributions to the global magnetic field and observe the resulting magnetic topology, including the formation of pseudostreamers, helmet streamer belts, HCSs, and coronal holes.
AI.result: When dipole and quadrupole contributions are approximately equal in magnitude, the model corona oscillates between one- and two-HCS configurations on timescales of days-to-weeks. The study characterizes the dynamical transition of a global-scale pseudostreamer into a localized, secondary helmet-streamer belt with its own HCS that surrounds a newly opened, opposite-polarity coronal hole.
AI.conclusion: The results have implications for solar cycle evolution and the dynamic coupling of the highly structured corona and inner heliosphere, suggesting that transitions between single and multiple HCS configurations are dynamically possible and occur on relatively short timescales near the dipole-quadrupole balance of the global field.

title: NGC 1901: A new benchmark cluster for gyrochronology in the TESS Southern continuous viewing zone
summary: We use Gaia DR3 astrometry and TESS time-series photometry to study NGC 1901, a sparse open cluster in the TESS Southern continuous viewing zone, that has been neglected due to its proximity on the sky to the Large Magellanic Cloud. We refine its membership list and measure rotation periods for 32 high-confidence rotating stars. By applying the gyro-interp empirical model, we calculate a gyrochronal age of 830 $\pm$ 50 Myr. Because NGC 1901 possesses a sub-solar metallicity of [Fe/H]$\approx -0.11$, its excellent agreement with empirical models suggests that temperature-period relations mitigate metallicity effects for Sun-like stars. Our results place NGC 1901 in the gap between the benchmark open clusters Praesepe (670 Myr) and NGC 6811 (1 Gyr). We find that the rotation sequence exhibits significant spin-down stalling in late K dwarfs, supporting models of core--envelope recoupling. Furthermore, our findings provide constraints for the cluster's structural evolution, including its recently identified tidal tail and corona. This study establishes NGC 1901 as a new benchmark for calibrating the next generation of gyrochronal models.

AI.tldr: The authors use Gaia DR3 astrometry and TESS photometry to refine the membership list of the neglected open cluster NGC 1901 and measure rotation periods for 32 stars. Using the gyro-interp empirical model, they derive a gyrochronal age of 830 ± 50 Myr, positioning the cluster between Praesepe and NGC 6811 in age. The sub-solar metallicity cluster shows excellent agreement with empirical period-temperature models, and they observe spin-down stalling in late K dwarfs that supports core-envelope recoupling models. The cluster is established as a new gyrochronology benchmark.
AI.motivation: NGC 1901 is a sparse open cluster that has been neglected because of its proximity to the Large Magellanic Cloud on the sky. As a relatively old cluster with sub-solar metallicity, it offers a valuable opportunity to test and extend empirical gyrochronology models in a gap of the current benchmark age ladder (between 670 Myr and 1 Gyr).
AI.method: Combined Gaia DR3 astrometry for membership refinement with TESS time-series photometry to measure stellar rotation periods. Applied the gyro-interp empirical model to the measured rotation period-temperature relations to derive a gyrochronal age for the cluster and to study the rotation sequence morphology including spin-down behavior in K dwarfs.
AI.result: A gyrochronal age of 830 ± 50 Myr was derived for NGC 1901, placing it between Praesepe (670 Myr) and NGC 6811 (1 Gyr). The sub-solar metallicity ([Fe/H]≈-0.11) cluster's rotation sequence agrees excellently with empirical models, suggesting metallicity effects are mitigated by temperature-period relations for Sun-like stars. Significant spin-down stalling was detected in late K dwarfs, supporting core-envelope recoupling models. The analysis also provides constraints on the cluster's structural evolution including its tidal tail and corona.
AI.conclusion: NGC 1901 is established as a new benchmark open cluster for gyrochronology, filling the age gap between existing standard clusters and demonstrating that current empirical gyrochronology models are robust across metallicity for Sun-like stars, while also providing observational support for core-envelope recoupling in K dwarfs.

title: The Role of Preceding CMEs and SIRs in Enhancing Shock Acceleration of Electrons
summary: The role of large-scale pre-existing interplanetary structures, including preceding coronal mass ejections (CMEs) and stream interaction regions (SIRs), in shaping the shock acceleration environment for energetic electrons remains not fully understood. In this study, we investigate nine interplanetary shocks observed by the Solar Terrestrial Relations Observatory (STEREO) that are associated with significant MeV electron enhancements, as such enhancements are rarely observed at interplanetary shocks. We combine remote-sensing observations, drag-based modeling, and in-situ measurements to analyze the shock propagation through pre-existing interplanetary structures. Eight of the nine events are associated with a preceding slow or intermediate-speed CME, while six shocks are in-situ observed propagating within preceding ICMEs, indicating that large-scale upstream trapping structures are a common feature of these events. Further analysis identifies three distinct scenarios associated with enhanced electron acceleration: shocks propagating through preceding ICMEs, shock-SIR interactions, and direct injection of flare-accelerated electrons into SIRs. As a representative shock-in-ICME event, the 2012 January 29 low-$β$, quasi-perpendicular shock ($θ_{Bn}\sim87^\circ$) is further investigated using observations together with one-dimensional Monte Carlo test-particle simulations of a shock propagating into a large-scale upstream magnetic loop. The simulation suggests that the upstream loop prolongs electron residence near the shock and substantially enhances acceleration efficiency. These results demonstrate that large-scale interplanetary structures can precondition the upstream magnetic environment, providing favorable conditions for prolonged electron residence and efficient shock acceleration.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates nine interplanetary shocks observed by STEREO that produced significant MeV electron enhancements, finding that eight were associated with preceding CMEs and six propagated within preceding ICMEs. Three distinct acceleration scenarios are identified (shock-in-ICME, shock-SIR interactions, and direct flare electron injection into SIRs). The representative 2012 January 29 shock-in-ICME event is simulated with 1D Monte Carlo test-particle simulations, showing that large-scale upstream magnetic loops prolong electron residence near the shock and substantially enhance acceleration efficiency.
AI.motivation: To understand how large-scale pre-existing interplanetary structures (preceding CMEs and SIRs) shape the shock acceleration environment for energetic electrons, since significant MeV electron enhancements at interplanetary shocks are rarely observed and their cause is not fully understood.
AI.method: Combined remote-sensing observations (STEREO), drag-based modeling of CME propagation, and in-situ measurements to analyze shock propagation through pre-existing structures. For the representative 2012 January 29 event (a low-beta, quasi-perpendicular shock with θBn ~ 87°), one-dimensional Monte Carlo test-particle simulations were performed of a shock propagating into a large-scale upstream magnetic loop.
AI.result: Eight of nine events were associated with a preceding slow or intermediate-speed CME, and six shocks were observed propagating within preceding ICMEs. Three distinct acceleration scenarios were identified: shocks propagating through preceding ICMEs, shock-SIR interactions, and direct injection of flare-accelerated electrons into SIRs. The Monte Carlo simulations confirmed that upstream magnetic loops prolong electron residence near the shock and substantially enhance acceleration efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Large-scale interplanetary structures precondition the upstream magnetic environment at shocks, providing favorable conditions for prolonged electron residence and efficient shock acceleration, which explains the rare occurrence of significant MeV electron enhancements at interplanetary shocks.

title: New scaling relations from MESA models for mass and radius of subgiant stars: application to Kepler targets
summary: The precise determination of the fundamental parameters of stars is crucial for understanding stellar structure and evolution. In this regard, the asteroseismic parameters of solar-like oscillating stars obtained from space telescopes are very useful for determining the mass ($M$) and radius ($R$) of single stars using classical scaling relations. These relations still need to be improved. In this study, we develop alternative scaling relations based on reference frequencies ($ν_{\rm min}$) due to helium ionization zone glitches, specifically for subgiant (SG) stars. We compile main-sequence and SG {\small{MESA}} models from the literature and derive new scaling relations for stellar $R$ and surface gravity ($g$) of evolved stars. The expressions for $R$ and $g$ are obtained simultaneously as functions of the large frequency separation, $ν_{\rm min}$, and metallicity. These new relations allow $M$ and $R$ to be reliably determined only from observational parameters, without the need for detailed stellar modelling. The resulting $ν_{\rm min}$-based relations are applied to a sample of 31 SG stars observed by the \emph{Kepler} mission, with masses in the range 0.85-1.74 M$_\odot$ and radii between 1.03 and 2.82 R$_\odot$. Using simultaneous solutions, we estimate new mass and radius ranges of 0.89-1.62 M$_\odot$ and 1.04-2.95 R$_\odot$, respectively. The results demonstrate significant improvements in the determination of $M$ and $R$ for evolved \emph{Kepler} target stars, highlighting the potential of the new scaling relations in asteroseismic analyses.

AI.tldr: This paper develops new scaling relations for subgiant stars based on reference frequencies (ν_min) from helium ionization zone glitches, enabling direct determination of stellar mass and radius from observational parameters alone. Applied to 31 Kepler-observed subgiant stars, the relations yield mass and radius ranges of 0.89–1.62 M⊙ and 1.04–2.95 R⊙, showing significant improvements over classical scaling relations.
AI.motivation: Classical asteroseismic scaling relations for determining stellar mass and radius still require improvement. The authors aim to develop alternative scaling relations specifically for subgiant stars using reference frequencies from helium ionization zone glitches, which can provide more reliable fundamental stellar parameters without detailed stellar modelling.
AI.method: The authors compile main-sequence and subgiant MESA models from the literature and derive new scaling relations for stellar radius and surface gravity as functions of the large frequency separation, ν_min, and metallicity. These expressions are solved simultaneously to obtain M and R purely from observational parameters.
AI.result: Application to 31 subgiant stars observed by the Kepler mission (input masses 0.85–1.74 M⊙, radii 1.03–2.82 R⊙) yields new estimated mass and radius ranges of 0.89–1.62 M⊙ and 1.04–2.95 R⊙, respectively, demonstrating significant improvements.
AI.conclusion: The new ν_min-based scaling relations show significant potential for improving mass and radius determinations of evolved Kepler target stars, providing a reliable method that requires only observational parameters without detailed stellar modelling.

title: Interferometric Survey of Stellar Parameters: Mass of the metallic A-type binary $β$ Aur
comment: 17 pages, 9 figures, accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: With the capabilities of the new visible CHARA/SPICA instrument and the multiple spectral band operation of CHARA, our goal is to resolve orbits of short-period binaries and develop a robust framework for combining interferometric, spectroscopic, and photometric observations into a single consistent model. For our target sample, we selected suitable binaries based on brightness, angular separation, and orbital properties based on the expected performance of the CHARA/SPICA instrument. As a case study, we analysed the bright eclipsing binary $β$ Aurigae, composed of two slightly evolved A1 stars. We combined new interferometric observations of $β$ Aur obtained with CHARA/SPICA, MIRC-X, and MYSTIC with archival MIRC data, radial velocities, and light curves. We first derived astrometric positions from interferometric observables and computed an orbital solution. Afterwards, we implemented a unified model, capable of tying interferometric modelling with the ellc code to simultaneously fit all observables using MCMC sampling. We performed a detailed analysis of the noise statistics of each data set and in the end we adopted a profile likelihood approach to account for underestimated noise and systematics. We derived a consistent orbital and physical solution for $β$ Aur through joint modelling. The inclusion of interferometric data tightly constrains the angular semi-major axis and inclination. Using profile likelihood to account for the different intrinsic levels of uncertainty of the fundamentally different observables, we derived the masses of the two stars, $M_1 = 2.359 \pm 0.005$ M$_S$ and $M_2 = 2.293 \pm 0.004$ M$_S$, their radii $R_1 = 2.752 \pm 0.002$ R$_S$ and $R_2 = 2.622 \pm 0.002$ R$_S$, and the distance to the binary, $d = 24.30\pm0.05$ pc.

AI.tldr: This paper aims to resolve orbits of short-period binaries using the new visible CHARA/SPICA instrument and develop a unified framework combining interferometric, spectroscopic, and photometric data into a single consistent model. Using β Aurigae as a case study, the authors integrate CHARA/SPICA, MIRC-X, MYSTIC, archival MIRC, radial velocity, and light curve data. They derive astrometric orbits, implement a joint model using the ellc code with MCMC sampling, and adopt a profile likelihood approach to handle noise systematics. They obtain precise stellar parameters: masses of 2.359 and 2.293 M☉, radii of 2.752 and 2.622 R☉, and a distance of 24.30 pc.
AI.motivation: The goal is to resolve orbits of short-period binaries and build a robust framework that jointly models interferometric, spectroscopic, and photometric observations into a consistent physical solution, leveraging the new capabilities of CHARA/SPICA.
AI.method: The authors selected suitable binaries based on expected CHARA/SPICA performance. For β Aur, they combined new interferometric data (CHARA/SPICA, MIRC-X, MYSTIC) with archival MIRC data, radial velocities, and light curves. Astrometric positions were derived and an orbital solution computed. A unified model linking interferometric modelling with the ellc code was implemented to simultaneously fit all observables via MCMC sampling, followed by detailed noise analysis and a profile likelihood approach to account for underestimated noise.
AI.result: A consistent orbital and physical solution for β Aur was obtained. Interferometric data tightly constrained the angular semi-major axis and inclination. Profile likelihood treatment yielded masses M1=2.359±0.005 M☉ and M2=2.293±0.004 M☉, radii R1=2.752±0.002 R☉ and R2=2.622±0.002 R☉, and distance d=24.30±0.05 pc.
AI.conclusion: The joint modelling framework successfully combines heterogeneous observables into a single consistent solution, demonstrating the power of CHARA/SPICA for resolving short-period binaries and yielding highly precise stellar physical parameters for β Aurigae.

title: Ionized Nebulae Around Two New Symbiotic Stars: GR Cygni and [D75] 141
summary: In the course of selecting targets for a spectroscopic survey of faint planetary-nebula nuclei, we encountered two anomalous cases of late-type variable stars surrounded by nebulosities discovered by amateur astronomers. We obtained follow-up deep narrow-band images of the two nebulae: StDr Objet 14 (diameter 1.5 arcmin) and StDr 4 (diameter 2.5 arcmin). StDr Objet 14 is found to be a low-excitation nebula, bright only in Ha+[N II], and showing a unique double-ring "bull's-eye" morphology. StDr 4 exhibits a bow-shock structure, bright in Halpha and [S II], embedded in an extended emission nebula. Both central stars, respectively GR Cygni and [D75] 141, are found to be pulsating semiregular variable stars. Our spectroscopic observations show GR Cyg to be a cool carbon star of type C9,2, with emission lines of the Balmer series, [O II] and [O III], [Ne III], [S II], and Fe II. A synthetic narrow-band image of GR Cyg shows that the source of its strong [O II] 3727 A emission line is a knot displaced from the star by about 1.6 arcsec, indicative of a recent collimated ejection event. [D75] 141 is a M6 III red giant, with weak Balmer-series emission. Both stars show a blue excess, and GR Cyg was detected in the near-UV by the GALEX spacecraft. These data establish both stars as new symbiotic binaries, containing a late-type red giant and a hot companion accreting from its stellar wind. We speculate that the double rings surrounding GR Cyg were ejected during helium-shell thermal pulses (or conceivably from recurring nova outbursts), while the nebula around [D75] 141 may be the result of a collision of the symbiotic star's ejecta with an interstellar cloud. Our accidental discoveries of these two binaries because they are surrounded by faint nebulae supports the view that there is a significant population of "missing" symbiotic stars yet to be discovered.

AI.tldr: Two late-type variable stars (GR Cygni and [D75] 141) initially mistaken for planetary-nebula nuclei were found to be new symbiotic binaries, surrounded by faint nebulae of distinct morphologies (double-ring and bow-shock structures). Their properties establish a hidden population of symbiotic stars discoverable via their surrounding nebulae.
AI.motivation: During target selection for a spectroscopic survey of faint planetary-nebula nuclei, two anomalous late-type variable stars surrounded by nebulosities were identified. The authors aimed to characterize these objects and determine their true nature.
AI.method: Deep narrow-band imaging of the two nebulae (StDr Objet 14 and StDr 4), follow-up spectroscopy of the central stars, construction of a synthetic narrow-band image of GR Cyg, and multi-wavelength analysis including GALEX near-UV data.
AI.result: StDr Objet 14 is a low-excitation nebula with a unique double-ring "bull's-eye" morphology, while StDr 4 shows a bow-shock structure in an extended emission nebula. The central stars, GR Cyg (a C9,2 carbon star with Balmer, [O II], [O III], [Ne III], [S II], and Fe II emission) and [D75] 141 (an M6 III red giant with weak Balmer emission), both show blue excesses. A synthetic image revealed GR Cyg's strong [O II] emission originates from a knot 1.6 arcsec from the star, indicating recent collimated ejection.
AI.conclusion: Both stars are new symbiotic binaries comprising late-type giants and hot accreting companions. The double rings around GR Cyg likely stem from helium-shell thermal pulses or recurrent nova outbursts, while [D75] 141's nebula may result from ejecta colliding with an interstellar cloud. The accidental discovery supports the existence of a significant undetected population of symbiotic stars.
